name: lz4_flex
baseline: lz4 (C reference 1.9.3, via the lzzzz Rust binding)
workload: LZ4 block compression and decompression of a 66 KB JSON file and the 10 MB dickens text file, criterion benchmarks in the repo's benches folder
claimed_speedup: 66KB JSON: lz4_flex unsafe 1615 MiB/s compress and 5512 MiB/s decompress vs lzzz (lz4 1.9.3) 1469 and 5313 MiB/s; 10MB dickens: 347 MiB/s compress and 2734 MiB/s decompress vs 324 and 2759 MiB/s (about 10% faster compression on JSON, decompression roughly equal; 'unchecked_decode' variant 5973 and 3168 MiB/s)
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.69.0 (2023-04-16), criterion via cargo bench --no-default-features (safe-encode and safe-decode features off); no extra RUSTFLAGS stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5900HX, Manjaro, CPU boost disabled, governor performance
tradeoffs: Rust crate, not directly callable from C++ without FFI. Fastest numbers need the unsafe (non-default-safe) build; the safe build is slower than C lz4 (66KB JSON: 1272 MiB/s compress, 4540 MiB/s decompress vs 1469 and 5313).
caveats: Own benchmark on only two small inputs; README numbers date from v0.11.0 (2023-06-02) with rustc 1.69; the win over C lz4 is small and in the safe configuration lz4_flex is slower. Tier A because benchmark code, rustc version, CPU and cargo bench invocation are public (no explicit RUSTFLAGS; default release profile implied), but the small inputs and the safe/unsafe split limit how far the result generalizes. The same README also lists lz-fear and snap.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github Rust OR Go OR Zig faster than zlib compression crate benchmarks' led to hwjsnc/rust-compression-comparison, which named lz4_flex; README opened on github.com

name: klauspost/compress (Go: S2, optimized deflate, zstd)
baseline: Go standard library compress/flate, gzip, zlib (deflate family); S2 also compared with Snappy and LZ4
workload: Drop-in replacements for Go's compress/gzip, zip, zlib and flate; S2 (Snappy-compatible LZ77 format) compression of a 4 GB web-page corpus and of a set of files, plus S2 vs Snappy decompression
claimed_speedup: README: deflate packages 'typical speed is about 2x of the standard library packages'; lzw '1.4-4x faster decompression and 1.1-2.7x faster compression' than compress/lzw; S2 on a mixed 4,014,735,833 byte web corpus, single goroutine: S2 936.73 MB/s at 73.60% reduction vs Snappy 790.15 MB/s at 71.89% and LZ4 452.02 MB/s at 73.50%; S2 'better' mode 451.10 MB/s at 76.05%; S2 compression vs Snappy up to 16.5x on 16 cores (e.g. github-june-2days-2019.json 16.51x, 15224 MB/s), 1.05x-1.91x on one core
hardware: S2 README: '16 core (32 thread) computer' (CPU model not named in the compression table); Ryzen 3950X (16 cores) named for decompression scaling
stars_or_usage: 5.7k stars; widely used in Go projects
tradeoffs: Go only (not callable from C++ without cgo/FFI); S2 is its own format, Snappy-compatible only in 'Snappy output' mode; fastest multi-core numbers come from concurrent stream compression using many threads; amd64 and arm64 assembly paths, with noasm and nounsafe tags to disable them.
caveats: The baseline is Go's standard library, not C zlib; no Go compiler version or flags stated; CPU model not stated for the 16-core table; the LZ4 row in the corpus table is an unnamed LZ4 implementation (likely Go); the ~2x deflate claim has no table in the README. Tier C because it is first-party with partial methodology.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github Rust OR Go OR Zig faster than zlib compression benchmarks' and own knowledge of the Go ecosystem; README and s2/README.md fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com

name: matbech/zlib (optimized zlib 1.2.11 fork, MSVC)
workload: deflate compression at level 6 of silesia/mozilla (51,220,480 bytes) and silesia/webster (41,458,703 bytes), x86 and x64 builds
claimed_speedup: silesia/mozilla level 6: zlib original 26 MB/s (x86) and 28 MB/s (x64) vs matbech/zlib 47 and 52 MB/s, with a slightly smaller output (19,064,581 vs 19,089,124 bytes); webster: 29 and 30 MB/s vs 38 and 43 MB/s (about 1.3-1.9x, derived from page data)
hardware: Intel Core i7 8770 (as written in the results file; the linked Intel page is for the i7-8700)
tradeoffs: Compression only (no decompression numbers); drop-in zlib API; targets Windows/MSVC and ARM64 with SIMD CRC and hash; the same table shows zlib-ng broken on x64 in that test.
caveats: Repository archived 2026-06-17 (read-only). Benchmark measured compression only, one level, two files, one machine; compiler flags unstated; built on zlib 1.2.11 which is old; combines Intel, Cloudflare and gildor2/fast_zlib patches, so the speedup comes from already-known forks. Footnotes in the results state the zlib asm baseline variant is broken.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github zlib fork faster than zlib inflate deflate SIMD optimized drop-in replacement'; README and Results.md of matbech/zlib-perf

name: NZ1 (NanoZip 1)
baseline: lz4 (also compared with zstd and ZIP)
workload: Not stated; README performance table only
claimed_speedup: README: NZ1 about 58% ratio, 2.8 GB/s compress and 4.2 GB/s decompress on x86 AVX2; comparison table lists LZ4 ~80% ratio, 0.7 GB/s compress, 5 GB/s decompress; Zstd ~60%, 0.5 GB/s, 1.5 GB/s; ZIP ~65%, 0.12 GB/s, 0.25 GB/s (so claimed faster than LZ4 at compression and with a better ratio, slower than LZ4 at decompression)
tradeoffs: ~500 line C99 library with AVX2/SSE2/NEON paths and CRC32 validation; configurable window 1 KB to 1 MB; aimed at embedded use.
caveats: No benchmark code, no dataset, no CPU, no compiler or flags; the LZ4, Zstd and ZIP rows look like generic typical figures rather than measurements (LZ4 at 80% ratio is not a normal result for LZ4 on text); a LZ4 'ratio' of 80% versus NZ1 58% is not explained. Same author as stb-zip, whose fast path was previously found to compute a different checksum. Keep as low-confidence claim; not independently verified; I did not read nz1.c.

name: pugz
baseline: GNU gunzip (gzip); libdeflate also compared in the paper
workload: Parallel decompression of gzip-compressed ASCII text files (FASTQ in the paper; 2.7 GB and 24 GB compressed files in the README), speed measured in compressed input bytes per second
claimed_speedup: README, dual Xeon X5675: gunzip 55 MB/s vs pugz 147 MB/s with 1 thread and 251 MB/s full decompression with 24 threads (1052 MB/s when only counting lines); i7-4770: gunzip 63 MB/s vs pugz 172 MB/s (1 thread) and 376 MB/s (8 threads). Paper Table II (32 threads, FASTQ files preloaded in memory): gunzip 37 MB/s, libdeflate 118 MB/s, pugz 611 MB/s, stated as 16.5x faster than gunzip and 5.2x faster than libdeflate
compiler_and_flags: README: make asserts=0 for maximal performance; compiler and version not stated
hardware: README: dual Xeon X5675 (2x 6C/12T, 32 GB) and i7-4770 (4C/8T, 16 GB); paper: 2x12-core 2.3 GHz Xeon E5-2670 v3, 512 GB RAM
stars_or_usage: 124 stars; paper by Kerbiriou and Chikhi (copy in repo at paper/paper.pdf)
tradeoffs: Only ASCII text files with bytes in ['\t','~'] work (no binary, no .tar.gz); no CRC32 check (README says adding it would cost about 33%); no multi-member gzip support; standalone program, not a library; output synchronization limits the in-order speedup; needs many cores to win (1 thread: 147 vs 55 MB/s likely reflects its libdeflate-derived inflate code, per the README).
caveats: Prototype, may crash or give undefined behavior with asserts off. Paper speeds write output unsynchronized to /dev/null, which the paper says mimics an order-insensitive FASTQ parser; the README full-decompression column keeps ordered output. The paper PDF text I read does not name its publication venue, so no peer-review credit is claimed; compiler version and flags are not stated. The newer project rapidgzip (already catalogued) covers the general case.
found_via: GitHub: WebFetch of github.com/Piezoid/pugz after searching parallel gzip decompression; README and paper/paper.pdf (pdftotext) read from raw.githubusercontent.com

name: fflate
baseline: pako (JavaScript port of zlib); README also says its compressor beats Info-ZIP and often zlib's ratio
workload: DEFLATE, gzip, zlib and ZIP compression and decompression in JavaScript (Node and browsers)
claimed_speedup: README table (pako = 1x): decompression 'up to 25% faster', compression 'up to 50% faster'; synchronous ZIP compression 'compresses both more quickly and with a higher compression ratio than most compression software (even Info-ZIP, a C program)'; asynchronous mode 'over 3x the performance of virtually any other utility'
tradeoffs: Pure JavaScript, so usable from C++ only through an embedded JS engine; 8 kB bundle; async mode uses Web Workers with about 50 ms start overhead per function; the README says outputs are checked to be no more than 5% larger than competitors at max compression.
caveats: The headline claim is against pako (a JS port of zlib), not against native zlib; the table gives only 'up to' percentages with no data, Node version, CPU or flags, and the benchmark results are not published (the README says run npm test). The 'beats Info-ZIP' and '3x' statements are likewise unsupported by tables in the README.

name: MinLZ
baseline: LZ4 (also compared with Snappy, S2 and gzip)
workload: Block compression of Snappy testdata files (e.g. protobuf, 16 concurrent threads) and compression of multi-GB streams (6.27 GB JSON, 2.6 GB Apache log, others) with the package's own concurrency
claimed_speedup: README: 'fastest mode typically beats LZ4 both in speed and output size'; protobuf block: MinLZ 1 27,837 MB/s compress and 17,613 bytes vs LZ4 0 12,649 MB/s and 18,766 bytes (but decompression 116,762 vs LZ4 137,553 MB/s, 'LZ4 is decompression speed king'); JSON stream of 6,273,951,764 bytes: MinLZ 1 14,921 MiB/s compress, 84.47% reduction, 3,204 MiB/s decompress vs LZ4 Fastest 5,860 MiB/s, 79.69%, 2,680 MiB/s and LZ4 Best 1,772 MiB/s, 82.60%, 2,694 MiB/s
compiler_and_flags: Go with AMD64 and ARM64 assembly; Go version and flags not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X 16-Core Processor, 16 concurrent threads for blocks; stream tests use the packages' concurrency
tradeoffs: Go package (C++ would need cgo or a format port); new LZ77 format with a fixed byte-aligned encoding, so streams are not LZ4 compatible; decompression is slower than LZ4 in block tests; MinLZ levels 2-3 trade compress speed for ratio (level 3 compresses at 210 MB/s on the protobuf block).
caveats: First-party benchmark by the S2/klauspost/compress author's circle; the throughput numbers add up many threads (block tests use 16 threads) so they are aggregate figures, not single-core; it is not stated which LZ4 implementation ('LZ4 0' and 'LZ4 0 (Go)' rows) is used for the non-Go rows; Go version and flags are absent.

name: Zippy (Nim deflate/zlib/gzip)
baseline: zlib (system zlib on Linux, through the nim-lang/zip wrapper)
workload: Deflate/gzip decompression and compression of small corpus files (alice29.txt, urls.10K, paper-100k.pdf, geo.protodata, a 'tor-list' file) timed per call with the repo's benchmark.nim
claimed_speedup: README: 'around 1.5x - 2x faster than zlib found on a fresh Linux install'. Table rows (min time, Zippy vs nim-lang/zip): uncompress alice29.txt.gz 0.233 ms vs 0.397 ms; tor-list.gz 27.297 ms vs 36.613 ms; compress best speed alice29.txt 0.643 ms vs 1.236 ms; tor-list 26.106 ms vs 178.197 ms; compress default alice29.txt 2.361 ms vs 5.726 ms
compiler_and_flags: nim c --gc:arc -d:release -r tests/benchmark.nim (Nim version and C backend compiler not stated)
tradeoffs: Nim only (callable from C++ only by porting or through Nim's C backend); pure Nim, no dependencies; handles deflate, zlib, gzip, zip and tar.
caveats: The comparison library is nim-lang/zip, a wrapper over the system zlib, so the system zlib version is unstated. The README's own default-level compress rows show Zippy slower on the largest file (tor-list: 409.542 ms vs 244.424 ms) and about equal on urls.10K (13.364 vs 13.049 ms), so the '1.5-2x' summary holds for small files and best-speed mode but not for default-level compression of large inputs. Nim version missing, which is why confidence is moderate despite the A criteria being close to met.
